---
title: "This is bananas: why you don't get arrays"
description: "Finding the avocado 🥑 in an array illustrates a core computer science problem: search. Arrays don't remember storage locations — you provide items and they forget where things went."
date: "2025-01-10"
image: "/blog/banana-as-question-mark.png"
imageAlt: "A peeled banana curled into the shape of a question mark"
authors:
  - name: "Ernst Stolz"
    avatar: "/avatars/ernst-stolz.png"
    xUrl: "https://x.com/hastoggle"
categories:
  - "Arrays"
---

The array is among the first data structures you meet when you come in contact with coding. Relatively easy to wrap your head around **on the outside**, it gets trickier on the inside — where methods like `filter`, `map`, or `find` do their work. Let's see why.

Take the `find` method, and the following array.

```javascript
const fruits = [🍑, 🍌, 🥑, 🍊, 🍉];
```

I'm looking for the avocado 🥑. Help me find it.

Sure — you can just **look** at the array, point at index 2, and be right: `fruits[2]`. With some seasoning, you'd enjoy your avocado.

## But what if you couldn't see where the avocado is?

```javascript
const fruits = [🙈, 🙈, 🙈, 🙈, 🙈]
```

The same fruits are still in the array, but now you're blindfolded and don't get to play peek-a-boo.

I'm still hungry 😋 — go find my avocado 🥑!

```javascript
const avocado = fruits.find((fruit) => fruit === 🥑);
```

Take the `find` method, and the following array.

```javascript
const fruits = [🍑, 🍌, 🥑, 🍊, 🍉];
```

I'm looking for the avocado 🥑. Help me find it.

Sure — you can just **look** at the array, point at index 2, and be right: `fruits[2]`. With some seasoning, you'd enjoy your avocado.

## But what if you couldn't see where the avocado is?

```javascript
const fruits = [🙈, 🙈, 🙈, 🙈, 🙈]
```

The same fruits are still in the array, but now you're blindfolded and don't get to play peek-a-boo.

I'm still hungry 😋 — go find my avocado 🥑!

```javascript
const avocado = fruits.find((fruit) => fruit === 🥑);
```

content.content:
# The hasToggle voice

Clear, funny, and confrontational — with the confrontation **covert**. The
exhibit titles state a belief the reader holds. That is the whole confrontation.
Nothing in the surrounding prose needs to press the point, and a label that
announces it ("MISCONCEPTION" in red above the title) kills it, which is why
that label was tried and removed.

This document exists because the voice drifts. It drifts toward prose that is
correct, defensible, and textureless — the register a language model produces
when a sentence optimizes for being unobjectionable.

Sections 3 through 8 are derived from lines actually written for this site and
actually accepted or rejected; §6 is that evidence. **Section 1 is different.**
The sources there were fitted to the pattern afterwards, so they describe what
the page aims at rather than what it has achieved, and §1 ends with the gap
between the two.

**How to use it at each stage.** Drafting: start from §2, the lines that already
work, and pattern-match. Editing: §4 and §5. Brainstorming: leave it closed.
Its instinct is to narrow, and applied to raw ideas it kills the ones worth
having before they are legible enough to defend. Bring it in when the idea has
a shape and needs words, not before.

---

## 1. Four registers and one stance

The page runs four registers. Each owns specific elements and has its own
source. A fifth name, Ford, is not a register at all — it is a constraint on all
four.

### The spine — Matthew Butterick, *Practical Typography*

The exhibit intros. Opinionated technical instruction: states that you are
wrong, explains exactly why, never hedges, never digresses, and does not soften
the correction with charm. The shape the intros already have — a rebuttal beat,
then mechanism, then a pointer at the evidence — is his.

> Safer than what? · You cleared it. Nothing refilled it. · Not any more. ·
> You need a function. · You'll design one.

### The walkthroughs — Brian Greene, *The Elegant Universe* (added 2026-08-19)

For mechanism passages, where an intro must carry an abstraction. Escort the
reader through it one step at a time: the concrete scene first, the abstract
word only after its referent exists on screen, and the reader told where to
look — watch, follow, notice. The scene extends the exhibit's own metaphor
(the bake gets a shelf and an oven), never imports a foreign one. Take
Greene's patience, not his scale: no cosmos, no wonder-hush, just the escort.
The tell that this register is missing: two unintroduced terms meeting in one
clause, asking the reader to solve a construction instead of watch a
sequence.

### The asides — James Mickens, "The Night Watch", "The Slow Winter" (USENIX `;login:`)

Steal the structure, never the voice — he is too distinctive to imitate without
it reading as impersonation. The structure: set up a received platitude, then
describe what actually happens in escalating operational detail until the
platitude collapses under its own specifics. **Texture is inventory, not wit.**

### The frame — Mary Roach, *Stiff*, *Packing for Mars*

The hero, cohort, digest and FAQ. Funny about technical detail without ever
being cruel about it, curious in a way that makes the reader feel invited rather
than tested. This is where the page is allowed to be warm without being soft.

### The instrument — Edward Tufte

Panel readouts and labels, and nothing else. Lowercase, middot-separated, real
identifiers, no adjectives, no jokes; every mark earning its place. In the
paragraphs this register comes out cold, and §6 records it being proposed there
and rejected every time.

### The stance — Paul Ford, "What Is Code?" (Bloomberg Businessweek, 2015)

Not a register. A constraint on all four. Ford's load-bearing move is that the
confrontation includes the narrator — he diagnoses the industry's impostor
syndrome and puts himself inside the diagnosis rather than above it.

This matters more here than it does for him. The misconception frame works by
quoting a belief the reader holds, and a quotation delivered from above is an
accusation. The moment hasToggle is exempt from its own verdict, the whole
device turns smug.

### Audit — 2026-08-16

These four are targets, not a description. The landing page was audited against
them and five gaps were found and closed the same day:

| Gap | Closed by |
|---|---|
| The stance appeared once on the whole page, in the hero footnote. All five exhibit intros diagnosed without ever joining. | Exhibit one now opens "We reached for it the same way, for about a year, before anyone made us say what it was protecting against." |
| Mickens covered two of five asides and they were **adjacent** — four and five ran the same inventory move back to back, the repetition §5 warns about. | Aside two becomes the inventory; aside five becomes warmth. The asides now alternate rather than doubling. |
| Roach never reached the exhibits. Intro three had no second person and no joke — the flattest prose on the page, structurally rather than by word choice. | Intro three now admits the delays are hardcoded, which is both the warm beat and a second instance of the stance. |
| "See? We told you what we're selling. Most landing pages hide that part." inverted the stance — the narrator awarding itself a point, and the only line punching at a third party. | Replaced with "Now you know what's being sold. Weigh the rest of the page against that." Judgment handed to the reader instead of claimed. |
| Aside two was the closest surviving thing to the aphorism §4 forbids. | Same edit as row two. |

**Re-audit before assuming this holds.** The counts that produced it are cheap
to reproduce: first-person plural per intro, register per aside, second-person
density per section. A register drifting back is invisible line by line and
obvious in aggregate, which is the only reason it was caught.

---

## 2. Lines that are right

The rest of this document is a filter. This section is the generator. When
starting from nothing, imitate these before consulting anything below.

> **For developers who learn by poking things.**

The whole voice in seven words. It names the audience by what they *do*, not by
seniority or job title, and it does not flatter them. "Poking" is the site's
verb — it appears in the hero, the CTA and the footer, and nothing else should
replace it.

> **Nothing on this page is a mockup. We checked twice.**

The fourth wall, opened for exactly one clause and shut again. The joke is that
the page knows it is marketing. Note what it does not do: it does not explain
the joke, and it does not follow with a third sentence.

> **I cleared the cache, so the page is fresh now.**

An exhibit title. Speech, not a proposition — a thing a person says out loud,
in the first person, in the tense they would say it. It is wrong, the reader has
said it, and nothing labels either fact.

> **Somewhere a tutorial is teaching you to build `/api/increment`. It will
> teach you to validate the request body, handle the 405, and write a fetch
> wrapper with a retry. All of it correct. All of it in service of adding one to
> a number.**

Texture is inventory. Three specific nouns do what no adjective could, and the
punchline is carried entirely by the gap between the effort and the payload.

> **cacheTag("landing-shell") · cacheLife("days") · one entry, shared by every
> visitor**

The instrument register, used in panel readouts and nowhere else: lowercase,
middot-separated, real identifiers, no adjectives, no jokes. This is where Tufte
lives. A readout that cannot be filled with true facts means the panel is not
finished.

> **The playground shows you the wall. The cohort gets you over it.**

The one place a two-beat reversal is earned. §4 forbids aphorisms, and this
looks like one — the difference is that both halves are literally true and the
sentence is drawing a real distinction between two products rather than
performing wisdom. Earn it this way or not at all.

> **One email a week. Unsubscribing is one click, and it works the first time.**

Warmth exactly where every other site is either cynical or corporate. It makes a
small, checkable promise instead of a large unfalsifiable one.

---

## 3. Techniques to reach for

**Texture is inventory.** When a line is correct but flat, the fix is almost
never a better adjective. It is more specific nouns, accumulated until the point
arrives on its own.

> Somewhere a tutorial is still walking you through `/api/increment`. Nothing in
> it was wrong. It just stopped being necessary.

becomes

> Somewhere a tutorial is teaching you to build `/api/increment`. It will teach
> you to validate the request body, handle the 405, and write a fetch wrapper
> with a retry. All of it correct. All of it in service of adding one to a
> number.

Nothing was added but detail. The joke arrived by itself.

**Comic understatement over severity.** The deflating aside lands; the austere
correction does not. "Grid users will be shown the door, politely, at build
time" survived. "Grid is not approximated, it is refused" was rejected.

**Break the fourth wall, briefly.** The `//` asides are allowed to know they are
marketing. "We checked twice." "You knew this was coming. We both did." One
clause, then get out.

**The asterisk substantiates. It does not deflate.** A footnote that walks back
the line above it costs the page the one thing it has — a headline you can
trust. So the headline makes the claim at full strength, and the asterisk hands
over the receipts: what to press, what to read, how to check. Same for "the fine
print:" openers on the demo asides. The small type is where the evidence lives,
not where the confidence leaks out.

**The aside lands on the exhibit's topic, not on its dependencies.** Demo five
spent its aside on Satori's missing grid support — true, useful, and about the
rendering library rather than about generating images from code. A constraint of
the thing underneath is not the argument. Implementation limits belong in the
panel readout, where they read as specification; the aside is for what the
exhibit is actually claiming.

**The reader is competent.** They have shipped something they could not explain.

content.content:
**The reader is competent.** They have shipped something they could not explain.
So has everyone. That is the premise, not the accusation.

**When a referent is vague, name it. Do not reach for a possessive.** "These
answer back" has no antecedent, and the instinct is to fix it with "Our demos
answer back" — but `our` repairs vagueness by asserting ownership, which drags
the sentence into vendor register. "The demos below" repairs it by pointing,
which costs nothing. This matters most next to a `we` that is being used for
solidarity: "So have we" makes the narrator a fellow sufferer, and a possessive
one sentence later turns the same `we` into the seller.

---

## 4. Do not

- **Label the confrontation.** No "MISCONCEPTION" eyebrow, no "here's what
  everyone gets wrong". The title is the confrontation.
- **Write aphorisms.** "An answer you read is borrowed. An answer you ran is
  yours." Rejected. Portentous two-beat reversals read as fortune cookies and
  are the single most common drift on this site.
- **Reach for Vonnegut.** Short sentence, then a shrug. This is now the default
  register a model reaches for when asked to sound literary. Using it makes the
  problem worse.
- **Stack DFW footnotes.** There is already a footnote layer, and the technical
  claims have to stay checkable.
- **Use the em-dash triplet.** "…what can read secrets, what can hold state,
  what ships JavaScript." Three parallel clauses in a row is the tell.
- **Flatter the reader.** "The fact that you're reading the fine print says
  something about you. Something good." Cut on sight.
- **Say "it's not X, it's Y"** unless X is a thing someone actually said.
- **Claim more than the panel proves.** The page's authority is that every
  sentence is checkable. One inflated line costs all of them.

---

## 5. Editing: three passes

Run these separately and in order. The Satori aside in §6 passed the first two
and failed the third for weeks, because they were being checked at once.

**Pass 1 — register.** Is it warm, plain and specific, or is it correct and
flat? Flat is the default failure, not wrongness. Fix with nouns, not adjectives.

**Pass 2 — truth.** Is every claim checkable against the panel directly below
it? The page's entire authority is that it can be verified, so a line that
overstates costs more than it earns. Read the readout and the panel copy
together; they have contradicted each other before.

**Pass 3 — subject.** Is the line about *this exhibit's argument*, or about
something adjacent — the library underneath, a general truth about the web, a
joke that would fit anywhere? Anything that would work equally well on another
exhibit is not doing this exhibit's job.

Then grep the draft for the tells: a two-beat reversal, three parallel clauses,
"it's not X, it's Y", a compliment aimed at the reader, and any construction
already used by a nearby exhibit. Reusing a signature move two sections apart
reads as a formula even when each instance is good.

---

## 6. Evidence

From the copy pass of 2026-08-15. Left column was proposed; right column is what
shipped after review. The pattern is consistent enough to be a rule: **the
warmer, plainer, more playful option won every time, and severity lost every
time.**

| Proposed | Shipped | Why |
|---|---|---|
| An answer you read is borrowed. An answer you ran is yours. | For developers who learn by poking things. | Aphorism lost to plain speech |
| Nothing here is a screenshot. Every panel is the feature itself, running. | Nothing on this page is a mockup. We checked twice. | Severity lost to the fourth-wall wink |
| Run the first one | Start poking | Same |
| It looks like CSS. Satori reads flexbox and nothing else — grid is not approximated, it is refused. | The fine print: it looks like CSS, but the renderer (Satori) only understands flexbox. Grid users will be shown the door, politely, the moment the route runs. | Austere correction lost to comic understatement |
| The playground shows you the wall. | Some things move faster with a coach. | Clever reversal lost to the plain statement |
| AI produces the artifact. You hold the meaning. | You get the playground and the making-of. | Portent lost to concreteness |
| Unsubscribing is one click, and nobody asks why. | …and it works the first time. | Cynical lost to warm |
| `MISCONCEPTION` eyebrow, red, above every title | (removed; topic restored) | Announced the joke before the title landed |

The right column is a snapshot of what shipped on that date, not a live citation
— several of these lines have been revised since, and the pattern is the point.

The Satori row is worth following all the way through, because it failed three
different ways in three passes:

**The reader is competent.** They have shipped something they could not explain.
So has everyone. That is the premise, not the accusation.

**When a referent is vague, name it. Do not reach for a possessive.** "These
answer back" has no antecedent, and the instinct is to fix it with "Our demos
answer back" — but `our` repairs vagueness by asserting ownership, which drags
the sentence into vendor register. "The demos below" repairs it by pointing,
which costs nothing. This matters most next to a `we` that is being used for
solidarity: "So have we" makes the narrator a fellow sufferer, and a possessive
one sentence later turns the same `we` into the seller.

## 4. Do not

- **Label the confrontation.** No "MISCONCEPTION" eyebrow, no "here's what
  everyone gets wrong". The title is the confrontation.
- **Write aphorisms.** "An answer you read is borrowed. An answer you ran is
  yours." Rejected. Portentous two-beat reversals read as fortune cookies and
  are the single most common drift on this site.
- **Reach for Vonnegut.** Short sentence, then a shrug. This is now the default
  register a model reaches for when asked to sound literary. Using it makes the
  problem worse.
- **Stack DFW footnotes.** There is already a footnote layer, and the technical
  claims have to stay checkable.
- **Use the em-dash triplet.** "…what can read secrets, what can hold state,
  what ships JavaScript." Three parallel clauses in a row is the tell.
- **Flatter the reader.** "The fact that you're reading the fine print says
  something about you. Something good." Cut on sight.
- **Say "it's not X, it's Y"** unless X is a thing someone actually said.
- **Claim more than the panel proves.** The page's authority is that every
  sentence is checkable. One inflated line costs all of them.

## 5. Editing: three passes

Run these separately and in order. The Satori aside in §6 passed the first two
and failed the third for weeks, because they were being checked at once.

**Pass 1 — register.** Is it warm, plain and specific, or is it correct and
flat? Flat is the default failure, not wrongness. Fix with nouns, not adjectives.

**Pass 2 — truth.** Is every claim checkable against the panel directly below
it? The page's entire authority is that it can be verified, so a line that
overstates costs more than it earns. Read the readout and the panel copy
together; they have contradicted each other before.

**Pass 3 — subject.** Is the line about *this exhibit's argument*, or about
something adjacent — the library underneath, a general truth about the web, a
joke that would fit anywhere? Anything that would work equally well on another
exhibit is not doing this exhibit's job.

Then grep the draft for the tells: a two-beat reversal, three parallel clauses,
"it's not X, it's Y", a compliment aimed at the reader, and any construction
already used by a nearby exhibit. Reusing a signature move two sections apart
reads as a formula even when each instance is good.

content.text:
Paragraph fixed (both the visible standfirst and the `metadata.description`, which carried the same sentence). The other two are design calls — options below.

## Headline

Today `/blog` mirrors `/lab`: `The blog` + **Articles.** vs `The lab` + **Contents.** The one-word-plus-period form is the house index grammar, so the question is whether to change the word or leave the form.

1. **Different word, same form — "Stories."** Warmer than "Articles.", and it's the standfirst's own noun ("deserve a story"). Keeps the rhythm across the two index pages. Cheapest change, but still a label rather than a claim.
2. **A sentence — "Web development, told as stories."** ← recommended. This line already exists in the file: it's the OG card title on line 20, so the card and the page would finally say the same thing. It states the lane instead of naming the bin, and it's a plain statement, not the two-beat aphorism voice.md §4 bans. Cost: `/blog` and `/lab` stop being structurally identical — one names a place, one makes a claim.
3. **Absorb the subheading — drop `The blog`, headline "Articles, in long form."** Removes the redundancy of a "The blog" eyebrow over "Articles." but reads flatter than either of the above, and breaks the eyebrow pattern every other page uses.

If the parallel with `/lab` matters more than the claim, take 1; otherwise 2.

## Image preview

The one post is 1536×768 (2:1) with `imageAlt` in frontmatter, so the data is ready either way.

- **A. Thumbnail per row** ← recommended. 2:1 image on the right of each list row (full-width above the text on mobile), inside the existing link. The bordered-list grammar shared with `/lab` survives, and it's the layout that still works at post #20. Downside: at ~14rem the banana is small.
- **B. Lead image + text rows.** Newest post gets a full-width 2:1 image above its title; the rest stay as they are. Strongest visual today. Downside: with one post it's just a card, and the asymmetry only reads as intentional from post 3 onward.
- **C. Card grid.** Every post an image card. Fixes bleak hardest, but drops the house list grammar and reads like a default blog template.

One a11y call either way: the image sits inside the same link as the title, so I'd render it `alt=""` on the index (decorative) rather than repeating `imageAlt` — otherwise the link announces the picture and the headline as one long name. `imageAlt` keeps doing its real job on the article page.

Say which of each and I'll build it.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that contact and blog already match the eyebrow+h1 pattern, leaving /lab as the last bare noun page to fix—and since the OG title mirrors the h1 on these pages, changing /lab's h1 means updating its OG title too. I'm brainstorming a few candidate headlines for /lab under the "The lab" eyebrow.

I weigh a plain statement about chapters running the real thing (checkable against the page, but risks repeating the standfirst), a line that names Next.js and echoes the site's "poke it" verb (though that verb's already used three times elsewhere), a version lifted directly from the standfirst's plan sentence (which would require trimming the standfirst, same as the blog fix), and a fourth option built around features running next to what people believe about them.

I land on the standfirst-derived option since it mirrors what won for /blog — reusing already-shipped copy so the page and card agree without inventing anything new. That means trimming the standfirst itself, and I work out the cleanest version: "Every chapter opens on something developers say — to ourselves, or to each other — and runs the real feature next to it. And as much of Vercel as can be proved from inside a web page." That reads better than my first attempt at the trailing sentence.

I note the OG title would shift to match, the tab title metadata stays as "Contents — the hasToggle lab," and I should mention in passing that /blog's tab title stays short deliberately. I'll present the three options with a recommendation, keep it tight, and flag that contact already fits the pattern while legal/masterclass sit outside this family.

content.text:
Blog page done and committed (`956b02c5`) — headline is now **Web development, told as stories.** (matching the OG card, which already said it), thumbnails are 2:1, right of the text on desktop and above it on mobile, `alt=""`. Verified in the browser at 1280 and 390; typecheck and biome clean.

Two knock-ons worth knowing: the standfirst's first sentence became a repeat of the new headline, so it's now "Written from experience, wrong turns included. Nothing is too out-of-scope to deserve a story." And the tab title stays `Articles — hasToggle` — the sentence is too long for a tab.

## The other pages

The eyebrow-plus-h1 index family is only three pages, and one already conforms:

| Page | Eyebrow | h1 | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/contact` | Contact | **Write to Eric.** | Already a sentence |
| `/blog` | The blog | **Web development, told as stories.** | Done |
| `/lab` | The lab | **Contents.** | The last bare noun |

`/legal/*` and the masterclass aren't in this family — different layout, MDX-driven titles. So `/lab` is the whole job.

Also worth naming: in all three, the OG card title is the h1. `/lab`'s is currently `The lab: contents.`, so whichever option wins gets copied there too.

**Options for `/lab`** (standfirst below it: "Every chapter opens on something developers say — to ourselves, or to each other — and runs the real feature next to it. The plan is everything Next.js can do, and as much of Vercel as can be proved from inside a web page.")

1. **"Everything Next.js can do, one chapter at a time."** ← recommended. Same move that won on `/blog`: it's already shipped copy, sitting in the standfirst's second sentence, so nothing new gets claimed and the card and page agree for free. Cost is the same too — the standfirst then needs that clause trimmed, becoming "…runs the real feature next to it. And as much of Vercel as can be proved from inside a web page."
2. **"Next.js, running where you can poke it."** Names the framework and uses the site's owned verb. But "poking" is already in the hero, the CTA and the footer, and voice.md §5 warns that a signature move reused two sections apart reads as formula — this would be its fourth appearance.
3. **"Every chapter runs the real thing."** Shortest of the three and closest in shape to the blog line. "The real thing" is vaguer than the rest of the page's prose, and it partly repeats the standfirst's opening sentence rather than the second — so the trim would have to come out of the better sentence.

Say the number and I'll change the h1 and the OG title together.

Checking contrast ratios: the current cyan-800/80 opacity fails AA at 3.22:1, solid cyan-800 is still borderline at 4.42:1, but cyan-900 passes at 6.36:1 and the currently-rendered muted-foreground passes at 4.59:1. I still need to verify the dark mode variant against its background before finalizing the merge fix.

Weighing two options: dropping the cyan classes entirely (zero visual change but discards the intended accent) versus bumping to solid cyan-900/dark:cyan-300 (passes AA and delivers the intended look). Since the user only asked to fix the cn merge order bug, introducing a visible color change is a design decision beyond that scope, so I want to flag this tradeoff rather than silently pick one.

I'll implement the bug fix while removing the failing cyan class so the page stays pixel-identical apart from the intended sizing/wrap corrections, then note the passing accent shade as an optional one-line follow-up.

But those size/wrap fixes themselves ripple across breakpoints — heading sizes shrink at sm/md on several pages, and the demo-section headings shrink noticeably at base, sm, and md too. These are legitimate consequences of the fix he asked for, so I need to flag them clearly rather than bury them, and quickly list out exactly which headings and breakpoints are affected.

The landing page exhibit titles going from 60px down to 36-48px feels like a substantial visual shift, even if it's the correct authored behavior — I should verify the landing page still looks right at desktop and probably grab before/after screenshots to show him.

I'll get an accurate comparison by screenshotting the current fixed state first at 1280px for landing and chapter, then temporarily stashing the fix with git to capture the before state, and restoring afterward.

With site navigation in the top nav, this bar is * pure in-page anchors — the shop window's own contents. */ const LANDING_SLUGS: ReadonlySet = new Set([ "boundary", "caching", "og-images", "server-actions", "streaming", ]); const CHAPTERS: readonly { href: string; label: string; n: string }[] = SHIPPED.filter((chapter) => LANDING_SLUGS.has(chapter.slug)).map( (chapter) => ({ href: `#demo-${chapter.n}`, label: chapter.navLabel, n: chapter.n, }) ); /** * The contents row, slim enough to pin. {/* The same rail grid the exhibits sit in: the label drifts into the gutter the ghost numerals used to hold (right-aligned toward the content, like they were), and the first link takes the content column's left edge — links are the row; the label is margin furniture.     {CHAPTERS.map((chapter) => (
  1. {chapter.n} {/* The rule draws itself in on hover — the same movement the reveals use, at link scale. */} {chapter.label}
    2. ))}
); }

Here's the full inventory, then the options.

## Where the numeral shows today

| Surface | What it renders |
|---|---|
| `/lab` shelf rows | `01` in a 2.5rem mono gutter, beside the belief, the topic, and a live reading from the running exhibit (`node v26.2.0`, `bake #bc82b2`) |
| `/lab` next-up row | `07` · topic · "lands Monday" |
| Landing exhibit eyebrow | `02 · caching & revalidation`, above the belief |
| Landing sticky contents bar | `01 The boundary`, linking to `#demo-01` |
| Chapter page-turn | `← 01 · The boundary` … `03 · The stream →` |

Plus two things that aren't visible: every landing anchor is `#demo-NN` (the hero's "Start poking" hardcodes `#demo-01`), and `syllabus.test.ts` asserts the numbers are zero-padded, strictly sequential, and match the contents bar. The digest email template doesn't mention chapters at all yet, so nothing outside the site depends on the numbering.

**What else each chapter already carries**, none of it arbitrary: the shelf it's filed under (`data & caching`), the topic (`server & client components`), the nav label (`The boundary`), the belief, the slug, status, and on `/lab` the live reading. No date is stored anywhere.

## Options

1. **Delete the numeral; let the shelf carry the structure.** ← recommended. Rows become belief + topic + live reading, the contents bar shows labels only, the page-turn reads "← The boundary". Anchors move to `#demo-boundary`, which also closes a latent bug: today renumbering would silently break every deep link and the hero CTA. Nothing on the page then implies an order that isn't real, and the registry keeps arrival order where it belongs — as array position, which is what `/latest` actually needs. The design work is the `/lab` row: the 2.5rem gutter goes away, so those rows need a new left edge.
2. **Replace it with the date it landed.** Add `landed` to the registry, render `2026-08-04` in the same gutter — the mono-date grammar `/blog` just started using. It's the one true fact about sequence, and it shows the weekly cadence the digest is selling. Costs: a wider gutter, six real dates to backfill, and evergreen chapters start reading as old.
3. **Replace it with the slug** (`boundary`, `caching`) — a real identifier, stable, and squarely in the instrument register. But it just restates the URL, and it reads as filing rather than reading.
4. **Number within the shelf** (data & caching 1–3). I'd reject this: still arbitrary, and inserting a chapter renumbers its neighbours — worse than what you have.

## The question underneath

The page-turn (`prevNext`) walks ship order too. If ship order is an artifact, the book's spine is currently arbitrary as well. Two ways out: walk the **shelf order** instead — the learning arc `/lab` already displays, which is a real pedagogical sequence — or drop prev/next and leave "contents" as the only way back. I'd take shelf order; it's a few lines in `syllabus.ts` and it makes the reading order mean something.

Say which option, and whether the page-turn moves to shelf order, and I'll do it in one pass — including the anchor migration and the tests that currently assert sequential numbering.

content.thinking:
I'm reworking the /lab row markers, swapping the chapter numeral for a subtle gutter tick mark instead, and thinking through how to align it properly using an aria-hidden span within the baseline grid.  I'm weighing whether to render it as an actual dash character or a middot rather than a plain block, since I want it to feel like an instrument readout mark and avoid visual collision with the bake stamp element elsewhere.  I'm settling on an en-dash rendered in mono font, aria-hidden, muted with a cyan hover state, since that aligns cleanly by baseline without extra layout hacks.  I'm reconsidering though: at text-xs a mono dash is only about 7px in a 40px column, so it might read better right-aligned or as a short literal hairline rule (like `w-6 h-px`) spanning the gutter, which would match the site's existing hairline border aesthetic better than a typographic dash.

Since the row has both a belief line and a topic line below it, I'm thinking about vertically centering that tick using self-center so it sits between the two lines rather than aligned to the baseline of just the first line, which could look more balanced against the two-line block.

Rather than trying to span rows, I'll go simpler: keep the tick aligned to the belief's baseline, same position the numeral occupied, using an em dash instead of an en dash since it draws a longer, more rule-like line within the cell.

For the next row that lands Monday, where the belief text is absent, I'll dim the same em dash to about 40% opacity so it reads as a placeholder consistent with the "lands Monday" label on the right.

content.content:
### The lab — site shape, 2026-08-20

The collection outgrew the landing page (half the syllabus is made of
routes — parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions — and
cannot run inside one page), so the playground has a book shape: a
contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`,
`/latest` redirecting to the newest chapter. One registry
(`apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts`) drives every list — contents
rows, the landing roadmap, the contents bar, page-turns, sitemap, OG
titles — so shipping a chapter is one entry flip: planned → next →
shipped, belief and navLabel added.

- **Chapter pages** render the same demo wrapper the landing shows, with
  the belief promoted to the page's h1 (the eyebrow demotes to a
  non-heading element). The frame adds the making-of aside (the folder's
  commit history + the checkpoints repo) and the page-turn row
  (prev · contents · next), and `/api/og` draws each chapter's card from
  its belief.
- **Index readings.** A chapter may put one true value from its running
  instrument on its contents row, each inside its own Suspense — the
  index is itself a partial-prerender demonstration. Truth rule: a
  per-visitor value says so ("your presses · 3"); a global-sounding
  count would be the index's first lie.
- **Vocabulary.** Visitor prose says *the lab* and *chapter* (voice.md
  §6, 2026-08-20). "Exhibit" remains the working word in code comments
  and these docs.
- **Shelves (2026-08-21).** Ship order is historical — "assume we've
  covered everything, and the order we covered it in becomes
  irrelevant" — so the contents page displays the collection by section
  instead: components & state / data & caching / routing & navigation /
  metadata & assets / the platform, carved the way the React / Next.js /
  Vercel docs carve the territory. Accession numbers never change when a
  shelf does; the landing roadmap stays flat.

## 5. Banked
--- 204 ---
## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

content.text:
All seven ref-truthiness errors are gone (`2f328049`). `noUnnecessaryConditions` is now clean across `apps/` and `packages/`.

**What was actually wrong:** Biome reads `useRef`'s *initializer* as the whole type, so `useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null).current` is inferred as `null` and `useRef(false).current` as the literal `false` — hence "always falsy". ## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and

trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

So Eric may want the visible number to hold its old value through the flip and only show the new one on settle, but that risks contradicting the demo's honest claim that React updates immediately, unless I can find a way to keep the state update real while just delaying what's displayed on the front face without it becoming a lie.

I think this is actually a legitimate device: the front face shows the "before" state while narrating a render that already happened, then the reveal shows "after" — as long as the copy makes that framing explicit. So I'll implement it by deferring the displayed value during a replay until the flip-back completes, while keeping the badge and annotations reading live values since those already name the real render. Then I need to double-check the intro and aside copy still matches this behavior — the line about the card turning over, replaying, then turning back with the number having moved should hold up.

Now I realize the aside claiming the new number existed before the card finished turning is even more literally true with this change. I'm restructuring the state so there's a real `count` driving annotations and replay, and a separate `shown` value that the front face displays — keyed to `shown` so the reveal wash plays exactly when the card flips back, which may make the earlier hand-restart trick unnecessary.

content.text:
Fixed in `520c4868`. The face now holds the old digit for the whole replay and changes it when the card is square to the reader again. **Two values, one truth.** `count` is the state — still updated on the click frame, still what every annotation reads. `shown` is what the face displays. Outside narrate mode they move together, so the plain counter is untouched: press, and the number moves immediately, wash and all. Verified both paths — narrate off goes 2→3 within 60ms with no settle; narrate on holds `0` for ~6s and then reveals. **The reveal got simpler.** Because the `

` is keyed by `shown`, the remount now plays the landing wash by itself at exactly the right moment, and the digits mount already wearing `ht-settle`. Both marks ride one commit — which retired the class-churn-plus-forced-reflow restart and the ref it needed. The wash also stops burning down behind a turning card. **One bug found on the way.** The replay used to end at the flip-back, but the reveal fires 550ms later, while the card is still rotating. A press in that window would set a newer count that the pending reveal then painted over — the number would go *backwards*. The guard now lifts at the reveal instead. Clicking every 200ms for eight seconds, the displayed value goes 0, 1, 2 and never regresses. **No copy changed**, and I checked rather than assumed. "Then the card turns back, and the number has moved" is now literally what happens — it reads truer than it did when it shipped. The fine print under the card ("the card can't actually slow React down — the new number existed before the card finished turning") is exactly what states the gap between the state and the display, so the hold isn't a claim the page can't back. The replay's annotations narrate the render that already happened, same as their siblings, and the face is edge-on the entire time they're on screen, so there's no moment where the card contradicts itself. `biome check` clean across 472 files, 220 tests pass, typecheck clean. `docs/design.md` §2 carries the rule this is an instance of.

## What this is

The approved playground architecture (design round 2026-08-20): a serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry. The forcing fact: at least 8 of the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions, ISR, navigation…) and cannot live on any single page.

Mid-build scope addition from Eric: the landing page speaks lab vocabulary too — "exhibit" is out of visitor prose everywhere ("chapter" for the unit, "the lab" for the place); it survives as internal working vocabulary in code comments and the design docs.

## Slices

- [x] 1 — syllabus registry (`lab/syllabus.ts`); contents bar + roadmap derive from it, landing byte-identical (tests pin the old literals)
- [x] 2 — the five demo wrappers extracted into their `(playground)` folders, chapter/topic/belief read from the registry
- [x] 3 — five chapter pages at `/lab/<slug>`: belief as h1, same instrument, making-of aside (folder commit history + checkpoints repo), page-turn (prev · contents · next), per-chapter OG card drawn by `/api/og` from the belief
- [x] 4 — `/lab` contents page (belief-titled rows, lands-Monday row, still-to-build `+` rows, digest capture) + sitemap entries
- [x] 5 — live readings on contents rows (one true value per chapter, each in its own Suspense — the index is itself a PPR demonstration; per-visitor values labeled as yours) + `/latest` → newest chapter
- [x] 6 — lab-vocabulary sweep (landing, FAQ, `/confirmed`, OG card), "A new chapter lands in the lab" re-anchor, contents-bar → The lab link, roadmap → contents link, decisions recorded in voice.md §6 + design.md §4

(3 and 4 were built in swapped order so contents links never 404'd.)

## Verification

Per slice: Biome + tsc + `bun test` in apps/web (209 passing, 11 new registry tests). Production builds after every route-shaped slice: all five chapters prerender for all six locales; `/lab` is ◐ partial-prerender with exactly one per-visitor hole (the press count). Browser-verified on the built app: contents rows render `node vX`, `bake #hex`, `400ms · 1100ms · 1900ms`, `your presses · 0`, `1200 × 630 · png`; `/latest` 307s to `/lab/og-images`; rendered landing has zero "exhibit". The shared-bake check (press rebake anywhere, the contents row follows — one tagged entry) is being confirmed on the Vercel preview per design.md §6, since `next dev` lies about cache semantics.

## Follow-ups deliberately not in this PR

- Chapter 06 (navigation & prefetching) claims the contents rows' hover-prefetch as its instrument — banked in design.md §5.
- Chapter-page Lighthouse pass (the `ht-reveal` at the top of a chapter page may want the landing's LCP treatment).
- Housekeeping surfaced during design: `apps/docs` is dead Mintlify boilerplate, `(counter)/` is orphaned, `/pricing` is off-voice next-forge boilerplate.

cat > /tmp/pr392-body.md <<'EOF'
## What this is

The approved playground architecture (design round 2026-08-20): a serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry. The forcing fact: at least 8 of the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions, ISR, navigation…) and cannot live on any single page.

Mid-build scope addition from Eric: the landing page speaks lab vocabulary too — "exhibit" is out of visitor prose everywhere ("chapter" for the unit, "the lab" for the place); it survives as internal working vocabulary in code comments and the design docs.

It kept going from there. The branch is now the pass that brings the rest of the site into the same house grammar — blog, contact, legal, nav, footer — ships chapter 06, and retires the chapter numerals.

## Slices

- [x] 1 — syllabus registry (`lab/syllabus.ts`); contents bar + roadmap derive from it, landing byte-identical (tests pin the old literals)
- [x] 2 — the five demo wrappers extracted into their `(playground)` folders, chapter/topic/belief read from the registry
- [x] 3 — five chapter pages at `/lab/<slug>`: belief as h1, same instrument, making-of aside (folder commit history + checkpoints repo), page-turn (prev · contents · next), per-chapter OG card drawn by `/api/og` from the belief
- [x] 4 — `/lab` contents page (belief-titled rows, lands-Monday row, still-to-build `+` rows, digest capture) + sitemap entries
- [x] 5 — live readings on contents rows (one true value per chapter, each in its own Suspense — the index is itself a PPR demonstration; per-visitor values labeled as yours) + `/latest` → newest chapter
- [x] 6 — lab-vocabulary sweep (landing, FAQ, `/confirmed`, OG card), "A new chapter lands in the lab" re-anchor, contents-bar → The lab link, roadmap → contents link, decisions recorded in voice.md §6 + design.md §4

(3 and 4 were built in swapped order so contents links never 404'd.)

## What landed after those six

**The lab**
- Chapter 06 shipped — useState & re-renders, with the card that turns to its own source and replays the click against it, annotated with values read live (`746fc10c`, `99bdf830`, `b391e71b`, `e066d6ca`, `4c6cc635`).
- The contents page is shelved by section, carved the way the React / Next.js / Vercel docs carve the territory (`8f4c83d3`), and its standfirst states the titling frame once, since an index of beliefs can't explain itself the way a running exhibit does (`7d37a9c3`).
- **The chapter numerals are gone** (`37b61a20`). A number only ever said which week a chapter got built — arbitrary, since the digest extends the syllabus in whatever order the work happens, and there is no chapter 04 in the Next.js or Vercel docs to match it against. The eyebrow names the chapter and its topic instead, anchors key on the slug (`#demo-caching`, which also survives a chapter changing shelves), and the page-turn walks `READING_ORDER` — SECTIONS, then registry order — so the book's spine is the learning arc rather than the build log. The `/lab` row gutter keeps its column and carries a status glyph: a hairline rule for a chapter that is here, a `+` for one that isn't yet.
- The lab headline states the plan rather than naming the bin: **Everything Next.js can do, one chapter at a time.** (`dcb745a6`)
- The state card's face now holds its number for the length of the replay and changes it when the card is square to the reader again, where the digits rise once into place (`fee011ad`, `520c4868`). The state still updates on the click frame; what waits is the display, and the aside's fine print is what states that gap.

**The rest of the site**
- Blog: reskin, standfirst, footer links (`512b57fb`), the article's layout restored and given its voice across five passes (`bca73927`, `2dfa1cda`, `af068009`, `fb66603f`, `8e8790e8`, `4f81178d`), and the index gains per-row thumbnails and the headline **Web development, told as stories.** (`956b02c5`)
- Contact: *Write to Eric* — a Server Action wired straight to an inbox, which is the mutation chapter's lesson doing its day job (`f01d1e5c`); replies come from eric@hastoggle.dev, and every plus in the frame is on the rules (`8d2afed9`).
- Legal: imprint and privacy under German law with real data, terms boilerplate deleted (`231ff07b`, `31959c29`); the demo cookie's stated lifetime is read from the code (`4fe62e7f`).
- One-click unsubscribe — a deletion, not a flag, removed from both stores (`8e84f2ba`).
- Nav: a real top nav for destinations, the theme switcher demoted to a footer pill, dark hover fixed, footer split into two categories and centred in its plus frames (`23e93c0c`, `3a8b71f4`, `2fd639ba`, `015244c6`).
- Route navigations open at the top; the anchor glide stays (`5e08812d`).

**Found on the way**
- `Heading`/`Subheading` called `cn(className, defaults)`, so twMerge resolved every conflict in the component's favour: every `text-balance` and `sm:text-5xl` passed to a Heading had been silently dropped site-wide — headings computed `text-wrap: pretty` and rendered `sm:text-6xl` (`9b6f26e2`). Visible only below `md`, where it was worst: chapter titles rendered 60px through the 640–767px band that asked for 36px.
- That fix made the landing digest eyebrow's cyan effective for the first time, at 3.2:1 on the tinted panel — under AA. It is now `ht-cyan-900`: 6.42:1 light, 9.81:1 dark, measured in the browser against the composited background.
- Biome's `noUnnecessaryConditions` reads `useRef`'s initializer as the whole type, so `if (ref.current)` reports as always falsy. The state cards' seven ref guards now compare explicitly (`2f328049`), and the last three lint errors went with them (`a05a470c`). `biome check` is clean across `apps` and `packages`.
- Housekeeping from the design round, plus the rest: Mintlify starter and `/pricing` removed (`dbd9fe7c`), the qa-stories lesson retired (`2e048e4c`), hello-world dropped and the CLAUDE.md docs block pointed at the bundled Next docs (`2125d057`), `.playwright-mcp` artifacts gitignored (`122c3e26`).

## Verification

Per slice: Biome + tsc + `bun test` in apps/web — **220 passing**, with the registry suite now pinning shelf order and asserting that no entry carries a displayable ordinal. `biome check` clean across apps + packages (472 files).

Production builds after every route-shaped slice: all five chapters prerender for all six locales; `/lab` is ◐ partial-prerender with exactly one per-visitor hole (the press count). `/latest` 307s to the newest chapter; rendered landing has zero "exhibit".

The shared-bake check ran on the Vercel preview per design.md §6, and it found something: **build workers bake `use cache` entries independently**, so the landing shell and `/lab`'s contents row each prerendered their own fingerprint, and a fresh deploy can serve two of them for "one shared entry" until the first tag revalidation or `cacheLife` expiry converges them at runtime. Recorded in design.md §6 (`befb1d3d`); the rule that falls out is that copy must not claim cross-page agreement for the static shells of a fresh deploy.

Browser-verified for the later work: blog thumbnails at 390 and 1280; `/lab`, both ends of the page-turn, and the slug anchors after the numerals came out; the contact aside's link; and the state card's hold-and-settle — a press every 200ms for eight seconds, with the displayed value going 0, 1, 2 and never backwards.

PR #392's body is updated. It now carries the six approved slices as before, plus a "What landed after those six" section (the lab's chapter 06 and the numeral retirement; blog, contact, legal, unsubscribe, nav; and the three bugs found on the way), a corrected Verification section, and follow-ups marked with status.

**One thing to know:** today's 8 commits are local only — `956b02c5` through `520c4868`, everything from the blog thumbnails to the state card's hold-and-settle. The body describes them, so it's ahead of what the PR actually contains until you push. Say the word and I'll push.

## Follow-ups

**Two still open:**

1. **The navigation chapter claims the hover-prefetch readout.** Can't be resolved here — that chapter is the one landing next, still unshipped. The contents rows already prefetch on hover via `next/link`, so the instrument is sitting there waiting for its chapter. Still banked in design.md §5 (reworded from "chapter 06" to "the navigation chapter" when the numerals went).
2. **Chapter-page Lighthouse pass.** Untouched — no commit on this branch mentions it and the docs don't record a run. The `ht-reveal` at the top of a chapter page is still the open question, since fade-ins defer LCP and the landing needed its own treatment for that.

**One resolved:** the housekeeping. `apps/docs` (untouched Mintlify starter, plant-store API and all) and `/pricing` (next-forge placeholder, linked from nowhere) were deleted in `dbd9fe7c`. `(counter)/` took a longer route: it was deliberately *kept* in that same commit, on the grounds that it wasn't boilerplate but the old Hazel useState lesson — then chapter 06 shipped the same lesson on the instrument grammar and superseded it, so it went in `746fc10c`, with its two revival paths banked in design.md §5.

**Also worth marking closed:** the old body said the shared-bake check "is being confirmed on the Vercel preview." It was, on 2026-08-20, and it found the build-worker divergence — each worker bakes its own `use cache` entry, so a fresh deploy can serve two fingerprints for one shared entry until the first revalidation converges them. That's recorded in design.md §6 and the body now states it as a finding with the copy rule that falls out of it, rather than as pending work.

## Details on call tree & network request formats:
Information on performance traces may contain main thread activity represented as call frames and network requests.

Each call frame is presented in the following format:

'id;eventKey;name;duration;selfTime;urlIndex;childRange;[line];[column];[S]'

Key definitions:

* id: A unique numerical identifier for the call frame. Never mention this id in the output to the user.
* eventKey: String that uniquely identifies this event in the flame chart.
* name: A concise string describing the call frame (e.g., 'Evaluate Script', 'render', 'fetchData').
* duration: The total execution time of the call frame, including its children.
* selfTime: The time spent directly within the call frame, excluding its children's execution.
* urlIndex: Index referencing the "All URLs" list. Empty if no specific script URL is associated.
* childRange: Specifies the direct children of this node using their IDs. If empty ('' or 'S' at the end), the node has no children. If a single number (e.g., '4'), the node has one child with that ID. If in the format 'firstId-lastId' (e.g., '4-5'), it indicates a consecutive range of child IDs from 'firstId' to 'lastId', inclusive.
* line: An optional field for a call frame's line number. This is where the function is defined.
* column: An optional field for a call frame's column number. This is where the function is defined.
* S: _Optional_. The letter 'S' terminates the line if that call frame was selected by the user.

2;r-124;update;200;50;;3;0;1;

Network requests are formatted like this:
`urlIndex;eventKey;queuedTime;requestSentTime;downloadCompleteTime;processingCompleteTime;totalDuration;downloadDuration;mainThreadProcessingDuration;statusCode;mimeType;priority;initialPriority;finalPriority;renderBlocking;protocol;fromServiceWorker;initiators;redirects:[[redirectUrlIndex|startTime|duration]];responseHeaders:[header1Value|header2Value|...]`

- `urlIndex`: Numerical index for the request's URL, referencing the "All URLs" list.
- `eventKey`: String that uniquely identifies this request's trace event.
Timings (all in milliseconds, relative to navigation start):
- `queuedTime`: When the request was queued.
- `requestSentTime`: When the request was sent.
- `downloadCompleteTime`: When the download completed.
- `processingCompleteTime`: When main thread processing finished.
Durations (all in milliseconds):
- `totalDuration`: Total time from the request being queued until its main thread processing completed.
- `downloadDuration`: Time spent actively downloading the resource.
- `mainThreadProcessingDuration`: Time spent on the main thread after the download completed.
- `statusCode`: The HTTP status code of the response (e.g., 200, 404).
- `mimeType`: The MIME type of the resource (e.g., "text/html", "application/javascript").
- `priority`: The final network request priority (e.g., "VeryHigh", "Low").
- `initialPriority`: The initial network request priority.
- `finalPriority`: The final network request priority (redundant if `priority` is always final, but kept for clarity if `initialPriority` and `priority` differ).
- `renderBlocking`: 't' if the request was render-blocking, 'f' otherwise.
- `protocol`: The network protocol used (e.g., "h2", "http/1.1").
- `fromServiceWorker`: 't' if the request was served from a service worker, 'f' otherwise.
- `initiators`: A list (separated by ,) of URL indices for the initiator chain of this request. Listed in order starting from the root request to the request that directly loaded this one. This represents the network dependencies necessary to load this request. If there is no initiator, this is empty.
- `redirects`: A comma-separated list of redirects, enclosed in square brackets. Each redirect is formatted as
`[redirectUrlIndex|startTime|duration]`, where: `redirectUrlIndex`: Numerical index for the redirect's URL. `startTime`: The start time of the redirect in milliseconds, relative to navigation start. `duration`: The duration of the redirect in milliseconds.
- `responseHeaders`: A list (separated by '|') of values for specific, pre-defined response headers, enclosed in square brackets.

content.text:
Both done. A production build is serving at **http://localhost:3100** — the readout is live on `/lab`, uncommitted (`prefetch-reading.tsx` + 4 lines in `lab/page.tsx`; `git checkout` and one `rm` reverts it).

## 1. The prefetch readout, previewed

The navigation row now reads `prefetched for you · 7 routes`, ticking up as rows scroll into view. It counts RSC payload fetches (`_rsc=`) off the resource timeline — no router hooks, nothing the page has to be told. Three things the preview settled:

- **design.md §5's premise is wrong in one word.** The rows don't prefetch on *hover* — they prefetch on **viewport**. Five routes were already fetched at load, before the pointer moved; scrolling took it to seven. An instrument built on "hover" would be claiming something the page doesn't do.
- **Requests aren't routes.** The first cold visit fired two requests per link — a ~0.7 kB shell, then the ~7 kB segment — so a raw count said "10" for five links. Deduped by pathname now.
- **Bytes vanish on a warm cache.** `transferSize` is 0 for cached responses, so the kB clause hides itself on repeat visits. The real version needs a decision: drop bytes, or label them "over the wire".

Also worth banking: prefetch is disabled in `next dev`, so this instrument can only ever be built against a production build.

## 2. The audit — chapter page vs landing

Production build, mobile 412×915, 4× CPU, Slow 4G.

| | LCP | TTFB | CLS |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/lab/caching` | **700 ms** | 9 ms | 0.00 |
| `/` (landing) | 824 ms | 4 ms | 0.00 |

**The banked worry doesn't happen.** At scroll 0 the chapter's top `.ht-reveal` is already at progress 1, `playState: finished`, opacity 1 — the element fills the viewport, so the `view()` range has elapsed before first paint. The chapter page is *faster* than the landing. Follow-up 2's LCP half needs no work. (Localhost TTFB isn't real; the render-delay share is the comparable part.)

**Lighthouse: `/lab/caching` scores A11y 95, Best Practices 100, SEO 100** — two real failures.

1. **Contrast on `text-muted-foreground/60` — 2.30:1 light, 3.35:1 dark**, both under AA's 4.5:1. It's the exhibit eyebrow's chapter name and the panel readout labels ("baked", "served"), plus ~10 other uses of that token. Only a full-opacity `text-muted-foreground` clears it: 4.74 light / 7.66 dark. Halfway doesn't — `/70` is 2.71/4.18, `/80` is 3.23/5.22. Not something the numeral removal introduced; that slot held the numeral at the same token.
2. **Heading order: chapter pages go h1 → h3.** The eyebrow demotes to a div under an h1 by design, so the footer's "Playground" / "Built in the open" are the next headings. `footer.tsx:12` h3 → h2 fixes it invisibly and keeps the landing valid.

**And the landing's 100 is an artifact.** At scroll 0 every `.ht-reveal` block — all five exhibits, the roadmap, cohort and digest — computes `opacity: 0`, so axe skips them entirely. The same contrast defect is on that page; Lighthouse just can't see it. Any future a11y run needs to scroll first or force reduced-motion, or it's auditing the hero, nav and footer and calling it the site.

Both fixes are one line each. Say go and I'll do them — the contrast one is visible (the dimmest labels get a step darker), so it's your call rather than mine.

This reveals a key methodological gap: Lighthouse only tests whichever single theme the browser's color scheme happens to be set to, so it can mask failures in the other theme.

To confirm this, I should rerun the audit with the color scheme explicitly emulated as light on /lab and /lab/caching — that's the rigorous way to check.

content.text:
Both fixes are in, and the fix turned out to be bigger than the two flagged nodes — `20b5da1f`, plus `22c52f7d` recording the method.

**Everything now scores 100.** Production build, mobile, 4× CPU, Slow 4G, **both colour schemes**: `/`, `/lab`, `/lab/caching`, `/blog`, `/contact` — Accessibility 100, Best Practices 100, SEO 100.

## What the fix had to cover

The two flagged nodes were `text-muted-foreground/60`, but measuring every dimmed sibling showed the whole ladder failing in light: **`/70` = 2.71:1, `/80` = 3.23:1**, and full `text-muted-foreground` is the first rung that passes (4.74 light, 7.66 dark). So `/70` and `/80` text went to full too — the lab's topic lines, the blog index date, panel titles, render badges, stream captions.

Then a **light-mode** run surfaced two more that the dark run had hidden: the lab topic lines at 3.23:1, and **"lands Monday"** at 3.22:1. That cyan moves to `ht-cyan-800` (4.56:1), along with the contact form's sent line and the era3 caption. The bake stamp and the Node version keep `cyan-700` — at 36px and 24px they're large text, where 3:1 is the floor.

Left alone deliberately: the `§` divider and the masterclass `·` bullet keep their `/60` and `/50`. They're aria-hidden pure decoration, exempt from 1.4.3, and dimness is the entire point of them.

Heading order: the footer's sitemap labels are `h2` now. Invisible, and still valid on pages that have real `h2`s in between.

## Two things about the audit method, now in design.md §6

- **axe never saw the landing page.** Every `.ht-reveal` block computes `opacity: 0` until scrolled into view, and axe skips invisible elements — so the landing's 100 covered the hero, nav and footer and not one of the five exhibits. The same defect was only caught on a chapter page because there the exhibit is above the fold.
- **The run inherits the browser's colour scheme.** The dim tokens passed in dark and failed in light. A dark-mode run called the site clean.

## The prefetch preview

Still live at **http://localhost:3100/lab** (that build includes it). I reverted the four lines wiring it into `lab/page.tsx` so the branch is clean, and left `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/prefetch-reading.tsx` untracked on disk as the seed for the chapter — delete it or keep it, your call.

The finding worth carrying forward: **design.md §5 says "hover-prefetch", and the rows don't prefetch on hover — they prefetch on viewport.** Five routes were already fetched before the pointer moved. If that chapter's instrument is built on the hover premise, it will be claiming something the page doesn't do.

content.text:
Done — `65a31f7f`. The row now reads **`lands Monday · 31 Aug`**, verified on a production build at desktop and 390px.

Format follows the readout register rather than prose: mono, lowercase lead-in, middot separator — the same shape as `bake · #53ae91` and the panel stamps. So it's "Monday · 31 Aug", not "Monday 31th August".

**The date lives in the registry**, not in a "next Monday" calculation. `NextChapter` gains `lands: "2026-08-31"`, because the date is a commitment rather than a derivation: if a week slips, the row should say the date that was promised instead of rolling silently to the following Monday and quietly pretending nothing moved. Promoting a chapter already means editing its entry, so the date sits where the status does.

It's formatted by hand from the ISO parts in UTC rather than through `Intl` — the row is prerendered, and a date that formats against the server's locale and then again against the visitor's is two different strings for one static row.

Two tests (222 total now): the next chapter's date parses as ISO *and* falls on a Monday, and the formatter handles the three shapes it has to get right — a two-digit day, a single-digit day, and a year boundary.

One thing worth your eye: the label will go stale on 31 August if the chapter doesn't ship or the entry isn't flipped. The Monday test won't catch that — it only checks the weekday, not that the date is still ahead. I left it that way deliberately, since a test that fails on a calendar date fails in CI on a schedule rather than on a change. If you'd rather the page defend itself, the options are a build-time assertion or letting the row fall back to plain "lands Monday" once the date has passed.

`biome check` clean across apps and packages, typecheck clean. The build at localhost:3100 has the new label; the prefetch readout is no longer in it, since I reverted that wiring before this build — `prefetch-reading.tsx` is still on disk, untracked.
